 DC's dry streak hits 10 days, with another week possible
 Sunshine and pleasant fall temperatures continue across the DC region, with little precipitation in sight through month's end and perhaps beyond.
 By 
 Ian Livingston

 We hit the weather jackpot, then kept on winning.
 The current streak of largely brilliant, sunny, and generally cool autumn weather began Sunday, Oct. 18 — the first day of this stretch with sunshine and no rain. Tuesday makes it days and the run is expected to continue through at least the end of October. 
 Since the 18th, seven of nine days have had below-average temperatures. The warmest reading has been 72, most recently on Monday.
 The Halloween forecast isn't looking too spooky, and a weak frontal zone passing through the region this weekend into early next week may or may not end the dry streak. The European model shown above keeps the area dry, while others, like the American GFS, bring some light rain by Sunday night or early Monday.
 Although the ongoing streak may feel lengthy, it's about what we might expect historically. Over the past 50 years, the longest annual stretch without rain has averaged about 17 days. Since 2010, however, it's been closer to 14 days.
 DC is running more than six inches below average for precipitation this year. ( Climate Room ) DC already had a longer dry spell earlier this year, going 20 consecutive days without rain (or snow) from Jan. 26 through Feb. 14. Baltimore also recorded a 20-day stretch, while the current run is on track to become the longest of 2026 at Dulles Airport.
 Dry streaks tend to favor fall's "nice day season, " with the main jet stream still to our north and the sluggish atmospheric currents of summer slow to fully give way. The longest without rain on record — 38 consecutive days — occurred from Oct. 3 through Nov. 9, 2024.
